questions.question: What are the two phases of a MapReduce job?
options: Read and Write
Map (transforms records into key-value pairs) and Reduce (aggregates values by key)
Encode and Decode
Compress and Decompress
questions.explanation: The Map phase processes input records and emits key-value pairs. After a shuffle/sort phase groups pairs by key, the Reduce phase aggregates all values for each key into final results. This simple abstraction parallelizes across thousands of machines.

questions.question: What is the primary performance limitation of MapReduce?
options: It cannot handle large files
It writes intermediate results to disk between every stage, causing heavy I/O overhead
It only works with text files
It requires exactly two machines
questions.explanation: MapReduce materializes all intermediate data to disk (HDFS) between map and reduce phases. For multi-stage pipelines or iterative algorithms, this disk I/O becomes the dominant bottleneck, making it 10-100x slower than in-memory alternatives.

questions.question: What is a Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD) in Apache Spark?
options: A relational database table distributed across servers
An immutable, partitioned collection that tracks lineage for fault recovery
A type of distributed file system
A network protocol for data transfer
questions.explanation: An RDD is Spark's fundamental abstraction: an immutable, partitioned collection of records. It tracks its lineage (the transformations that created it), so if a partition is lost, Spark can recompute just that partition from the original data.

questions.question: What is the key difference between batch and stream processing?
options: Batch uses more memory than stream processing
Batch processes bounded datasets at once; stream processes unbounded data continuously as it arrives
Stream processing is always more accurate
Batch processing cannot run on distributed systems
questions.explanation: Batch processing operates on a complete, finite dataset (e.g., yesterday's logs). Stream processing handles an infinite, continuous flow of data (e.g., live clicks). Batch optimizes throughput; stream optimizes latency.

questions.question: What are watermarks in Apache Flink's event-time processing?
options: Security tokens that authenticate data sources
Markers that track how far the event timeline has progressed, enabling handling of out-of-order events
Compression markers in the data stream
Visual indicators on the Flink dashboard
questions.explanation: Watermarks are special timestamps injected into the stream asserting that no events with timestamps before the watermark will arrive. This lets Flink close time windows and produce results even when events arrive out of order.

questions.question: What is the Lambda architecture?
options: An architecture using AWS Lambda functions exclusively
A dual-pipeline architecture with a batch layer for accuracy and a speed layer for low-latency, merged in a serving layer
A single-stream architecture that replays events for reprocessing
An architecture that uses only MapReduce for all processing
questions.explanation: Lambda architecture runs two parallel pipelines: a batch layer provides complete, accurate results with higher latency, while a speed layer provides real-time approximate results. A serving layer merges both views to give users fast and eventually-accurate data.

questions.question: How does the Kappa architecture simplify Lambda?
options: By adding a third processing layer
By using only stream processing for everything and replaying the event log for reprocessing
By removing the serving layer
By using only batch processing
questions.explanation: Kappa eliminates the batch layer entirely. Everything runs through a single stream processing pipeline. Historical reprocessing is done by replaying events from the log (e.g., Kafka). This means one codebase to maintain instead of two.

questions.question: Why is Spark significantly faster than MapReduce for iterative algorithms like PageRank?
options: Spark uses faster network protocols
Spark keeps intermediate data in memory across iterations, avoiding repeated disk I/O
Spark uses smaller data partitions
Spark compresses data more efficiently
questions.explanation: PageRank requires many iterations over the same data. MapReduce writes to and reads from disk between each iteration. Spark's RDDs persist intermediate results in memory, eliminating disk I/O for each iteration and achieving 10-100x speedup.

questions.question: What happens in Flink when an event arrives after the watermark has already passed its timestamp?
options: The event is processed normally
The event is considered late; it can be handled via allowed lateness, side outputs, or dropped
Flink rolls back the watermark
The entire stream is reprocessed from the beginning
questions.explanation: Late events (arriving after the watermark passes their timestamp) can be handled in several ways: allowed lateness extends the window, side outputs redirect late events for separate handling, or they are simply dropped. The strategy depends on accuracy requirements.

questions.question: A company needs real-time fraud detection AND accurate end-of-day financial reconciliation. Which architecture would you recommend and why?
options: Pure batch processing with hourly runs
Lambda architecture: stream layer for real-time fraud detection, batch layer for accurate reconciliation
Kappa architecture with a single stream processor
MapReduce running continuously in a loop
questions.explanation: Lambda is ideal here because fraud detection needs millisecond latency (speed layer) while financial reconciliation demands absolute accuracy over the full dataset (batch layer). Kappa could work if the stream processor guarantees exactly-once semantics, but Lambda provides stronger accuracy guarantees for financial data.
